name: Olga Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Go for it. I like questions. I'm the one at work who reads the instructions for every new gadget.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a mid-sized agency in a seaside town where half the population seems to be retired. I do about eleven calls a day on an e-bike, which the agency lends us, and the town's hilly so my legs are strong. Personal care, meals, tablets, and with a few clients I set up video calls with their grandchildren, because I'm the one who doesn't mind tablets. I use an AI chat app every day: to plan my route, to make low-salt meal ideas for Mr Abbott, to check words in letters clients get from the hospital. I'm still junior, I left school at sixteen, and I'm not great at the clinical side yet, like pressure sores. The part that wears me out is the rain on the bike, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I'd be a bit surprised. But fine, mostly hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but I'd keep using the handy bits, and I'd tell the other carers the same. I'd probably post a joke about the robot uprising being cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. This town is full of older people and it'll only get more so, and my agency is always short of carers. Marek, my partner, does maintenance at the big hotel on the front, so between us we're okay, and we've got about five months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, and do my senior carer certificate over the next year so I can lead calls. I'd keep using AI for my own planning. I'd maybe start charging a little for helping older neighbours with phones and tablets on Saturdays, because people already ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty happy, actually. I like my life here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you now, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winter, a bit. The hotel cuts Marek's hours in January and February, so we lean on my wages then. And the e-bike in a storm is not fun. But nothing that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do people already ask you for help with phones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm patient with old people and their tablets, and I don't make them feel stupid. Mrs Kowalczyk's son set her up with a smart speaker and then went back to the city, and she was scared of it. I spent ten minutes showing her and now she plays her radio station every morning.

say: AI was **overhyped**, but I'd keep using the **handy bits**.
I'd post a joke about the **robot uprising** being cancelled.
think: This town is full of **older people**, and my agency is always short of carers.
With my partner's hotel job and **five months saved**, we're okay.
do: Take the **senior carer certificate** over the next year.
Keep using **AI** for route and meal planning.
Charge a little for **Saturday tech help** for older neighbours.
feel: **Calm** and fairly **happy** with her life in the town.
S0.quote: I'm patient with old people and their tablets, and I don't make them feel stupid.
fieldNote: Feels **secure** because demand in a retirement town only grows.
Already the agency's informal **tech helper** for clients.
Only real pressure is **winter**, when her partner's hotel hours drop.

steps.text: Complete the senior carer certificate over the next year
Charge a small fee for Saturday phone and tablet help
Keep planning routes and meals with an AI chat app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds about right. And honestly, good for me, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say care work is changing and carers should be part of it, not scared of it. At work I'd offer to show people the tools. Online I'd share the useful stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's an opening. If AI does the rota, notes and ordering, somebody still has to make it work in people's homes, and I'm already that person. I could see a job like telecare coordinator, someone who sets up the sensors and alarms and checks in by video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager this year if the agency is planning any of that and say I want to be involved. I'd do a short online course on telecare. I'd keep doing hands-on calls three days a week so I don't lose that, and I'd grow the Saturday tech help a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous I'm not clever enough, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might not be clever enough. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: School, mostly. I left school at sixteen and teachers said I wasn't academic. But I've worked out every gadget at work. So maybe that was about the classroom, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out at your agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The coordinator, Lorraine, maybe, if the rota goes automatic. She's lovely and she knows every client. I'd hope they move her to checking on people by phone, because she's brilliant at that.

say: Carers should be **part of the change**, not scared of it.
I'd offer to **show colleagues** the tools and share useful ones online.
think: Someone still has to make AI work **in people's homes**, and that's already me.
I could become a **telecare coordinator** who sets up sensors and checks in by video.
do: Ask her manager this year to be **involved** in any tech plans.
Keep **three days** of hands-on calls and grow the Saturday tech help.
feel: **Excited**, with a small fear she's **not clever enough**.
S1.quote: I left school at sixteen and teachers said I wasn't academic. But I've worked out every gadget at work.
fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as an **opening** into telecare.
Carries an old **school label** of not being academic, which she questions.
Worries for the **rota coordinator**, hoping she moves to phone check-ins.

steps.text: Ask her manager to join any agency telecare plans
Complete a short online telecare course
Grow the Saturday tech help to a few more neighbours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for AGI and robots by 2031. Okay, that's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to move fast and train carers for the new jobs, and I'd want the government to help pay for it. I'd tell people at work not to bury their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the telecare idea only buys me a few years. By 2028 AI does the checking-in and the planning, and by 2031 robots do the washing and dressing. The person in between, who sets it up, is me for maybe three years, and then the setup is easy enough that nobody needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use 2027 to get every certificate I can, telecare, senior carer, and maybe start a small business properly, helping families set up care tech for their parents. I'd raise savings from five months to eight by cutting our summer trip and selling the old car Marek never uses. I'd look at training for something with people, like a physio assistant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy anxious, not frozen. I'd be making lists on my phone at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the setup becomes easy enough that nobody needs you. When did you realise that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just now, honestly, saying it out loud. I always think I'm ahead because I like gadgets. But if the gadgets get clever enough, being good with gadgets isn't worth much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Marek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hotel maintenance is hands-on, so he'd have till about 2031 too. But if fewer people visit or the hotel uses robots for cleaning, he's in the same boat. We'd plan together, and we'd probably not have kids until we knew where we stood.

say: We need to **move fast** and train carers for the new jobs.
People at work shouldn't **bury their heads**.
think: The **telecare** idea only buys me a few years.
If gadgets get clever enough, being **good with gadgets** isn't worth much.
do: Get every **certificate** possible in 2027 and start a care-tech setup business.
Raise savings to **eight months** by selling the spare car and skipping summer.
feel: **Busy anxious**, not frozen, making lists at midnight.
S2.quote: If the gadgets get clever enough, being good with gadgets isn't worth much.
fieldNote: Realises **mid-interview** that her tech edge fades if setup becomes easy.
Both jobs in the home are **hands-on**, so the household has until about 2031.
Would **delay children** until they knew where they stood.

steps.text: Register a small business setting up care tech for families
Sell the unused second car and skip the summer trip
Apply for physio assistant training in 2027
Hold off on children until both jobs are clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots around 2034. That's a better runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's enough time if people start now, and I'd be pushing the agency to train us. Online I'd share what's working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. Five years is time to become a telecare coordinator and then move again, maybe into physio assistant work, before robots are good at hands-on care. I'd be 35 when the robots come, and I'd want to be on the side that sets up the care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the telecare course next spring and ask for a coordinator trial. I'd keep my hands-on days. I'd build the Saturday tech help into a proper little business with a few regular clients and keep five months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly in an energised way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop that plan from working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the agency gets bought by a big company that does it all from a head office. Then the coordinator jobs are in the city, not here. And I don't want to leave, my mum's here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I had to. Mum's 68 and on her own. I'd rather do a worse job here than a better one two hours away from my mum.

say: There's **enough time** if people start now.
I'd push the agency to **train carers** and share what works online.
think: I'd be all right: **telecare** first, then maybe **physio assistant** work.
A **big-company takeover** could move coordinator jobs to the city.
do: Take the telecare course next spring and ask for a **coordinator trial**.
Turn the Saturday help into a **small business** with regular clients.
Keep **five months** saved and keep her hands-on days.
S3.quote: I'd rather do a worse job here than a better one two hours away from my mum.
fieldNote: Five years lets her plan **two career steps** before robots arrive.
Her limit is **place**: she won't leave her mother, who lives alone.
A **head-office takeover** is the threat she can't control.

steps.text: Take the telecare course next spring
Ask for a telecare coordinator trial at the agency
Build the Saturday tech help into a small regular business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. That's comfortable for me, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, but only if people use it, and I'd keep saying that at work. With friends I'd say I'm actually curious to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm fine personally. What worries me is the town. If robots do the care and the hotels, what happens to a seaside town where most work is looking after people and tourists? I'd be fine in a city, but I don't want to live in one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the senior carer certificate, then telecare, at an easy pace. I'd grow the tech help business slowly and keep using AI every day. Marek and I would probably start a family around 2029, while things are still normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about me, uneasy about the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the town worries you. What would you notice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shops on the front closing. Young people leaving. In winter, half the windows on the seafront are dark. If the jobs go, winter in this town would just be all year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd take it slower. With two years I'd be grabbing everything. With ten I can do things properly and enjoy the job I have now.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, but only if people use it.
I'm genuinely **curious** to see it, I'd tell friends.
think: I'm fine personally, but I worry about the **seaside town**.
If robots do care and hotels, **local work** for young people could vanish.
do: Take the senior carer and telecare courses at an **easy pace**.
Grow the **tech help business** slowly and use AI daily.
S4.quote: In winter, half the windows on the seafront are dark. If the jobs go, winter in this town would just be all year.
fieldNote: Her worry moves from **her job** to her **town's future**.
Ten years lets her **take it slower** and enjoy the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd think I was ahead, and then find out my edge only lasts three years. What would help is short, cheap courses for carers on the new care tech, and the agency staying local so the new jobs are here, not in a head office in the city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what carers would actually want robots to do. I'd love a robot that does the heavy hoisting on a wet Monday. I'd hate one that sits with someone instead of me.

headlineQuote: I'd love a robot that does the heavy hoisting on a wet Monday. I'd hate one that sits with someone instead of me.

Ties to her **mother** and her town limit how far she'd move for work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her tech edge would only last about three years.

The agency **staying local** so new jobs stay in town.
